The three core primitives—opponent-adjusted efficiency, turnover regression, and explosive-play differential—are designed to capture distinct aspects of performance variation. Opponent-adjusted efficiency uses a linear shrinkage model to correct for variance due to defensive strength, assuming that observed performance can be decomposed into skill and luck components. Turnover regression applies a similar shrinkage approach to intercept rate, leveraging historical averages to reduce noise in small-sample estimates. Explosive-play differential isolates high-leverage plays through a ratio-based normalization, capturing strategic impact. These primitives form a coherent kernel for Bayesian updating in GSI, where each contributes a dimensionally consistent signal to a composite efficiency score. Dualities emerge in how each primitive balances empirical data against prior expectations, with failure modes including overfitting to short-term trends or underweighting rare but impactful events such as turnovers or explosive plays. The system must maintain coherence across these signals to avoid spurious correlations or misalignment in predictive models.
